Since we used the catalysts for electrolysis on CO2 while dissolved in heavy water, we prepared them on a carbon paper substrate, soaked in a Molybdenum ion solution run through a PECVD process alongside a precursor to make an array of Pr N Graphene:MoS2 and G N Graphene:MoS2 MXene nano structures on the surface of the electrode. Then a high power laser and flash joule heating was used to carbonize excess carbon and molybdenum to form small amounts of Mo2C which improved adsorption of CO2 at active sites with an effect kind of like a transistor due to the earlier Pr N doping and MoS2+Carbon layer which made energy transfer more favorable, allowing us to break down the CO2 and form larger organic molecules. We mainly targeted formaldehyde and i think methane, but I remember alcohol being a side product! Your catalysts and methods to select alcohol is definitely a lot more exotic, but super cool to see similar ideas from niche research on a huge channel.

To be clear, he wouldn't die a slow death from the actual acid burns (though those would be bad). HF actually kills because of the massive influx of fluoride ions into the body, which bind to and sequester calcium ions in the blood.

Without calcium ions, many important cellular processes such as nerve membrane repolarization and muscle contraction can't occur, hence death. In fact, death from HF exposure can occur from as little as 1-2% of skin coverage, or a small splash, depending on the concentration, time of exposure, etc.

Another fun fact, HF is technically a "weak acid" by definition because the hydronium ions do not completely dissociate in water ("weak" and "strong" in this context refer to extent of ion dissociation, not damage potential, though the two can be related). For a weak acid, though, HF is indeed extremely dangerous.

So cryogenics engineer here. Couple of notes:

1. Safety: The danger in handeling cryogenic fluids lies among others in the chance for frostbite, but particular in its capability to explode or suffocate living beings. If for any reason, the "thermal integrity" is broken (i.e., loss of vacuum seal), it results in rapid vaporization of your cryogenic fluid. If it is a closed vessel, you're waiting for an explosion to happen. For this reason, it is extremely important to place pressure relieve valves/burst disks on every closed volume. Besides the explosion, suffocation is also no joke. If 100L of LN2 evaporates. it fills a room of about 5x5m with a height of 2.4m. While a O2 sensor won't help you in case of an explosion, it will warn you in case of a leak.
2. Construction: That gasket between your flange and the "dewar" is made out of TPU which is unlikely to hold cryogenic temperature. Switch that out for something like a conflat.
3. Dewar: so I'm quite certain that dewar you have is more a cryostat used for experimental physics. I.e., you load it with an experiment which you would like to perform at temperatures of your cryogenic bath (i.e., LHe or LN2 temperatures), you fill it with said cryogen and run the experiments. This I think because its a top loaded tube and its a tube. Tubes are not great at handling high pressures due to the sharp corners at the top and bottom. Dewars should be able to handle high pressures because you usually extract some cryogen by evaporating a bit of liquid which increases the pressure. This pressure increase then pushes out the cryogen through the extraction tube as seen in this video. I would very much advise against pressurizing this vessel because it is not meant for this application. 
4. Liquid Helium: So you mention that you want to make LHe with this setup in the future. Be cautious that this requires significantly more energy (read up on Carnot on wiki). Furthermore it requires much better heat management because of this reduced efficiency and poses some additional risks. Besides He3 and He4, all other substances are in the solid state at 4.2K. This means that any foreign substances can clog your system, causing an enclosed volume which in turn is a safety risk. 

So there's probably much more to talk about, but be aware that because your setup performed safely once, it might not indefinetely. Structural failures can happen over time, i.e., metal fatigue, embrittlement, etc.

You definitely did a lot of homework off camera to get these annoying and complex systems working without them having a fit. 
On the topic of patience, when and MRI magnet goes "warm" after venting it's helium during a quench and sitting long enough to reach near room temp it takes several days and multiple gas steps to cool the vessel back down to store liquid helium. These things are very slow processes but they always get there eventually. 

My only advice (if you happen to read this) is that the compressor has an adsorber in it (the big black metal cylinder inside) and it needs to be replaced every ~3 years in my field. You could probably double that without any issues but if you want to play it safe, 3 is a good bet. Without replacement it can cause oil buildup in the lines and kill the cold head and/or compressor. 

Also those cold head degrade over time so you might not be able to reach liquid helium temps with that one anymore. It'll be more than good enough for nitrogen and oxygen for years though.

The reason this case makes me uncomfortable is that the vacuum jacket is, of course under vacuum. If the pressure difference is enough to cause the inner wall of that dewar to touch the outer wall bridging the vacuum jacket gap, it could flash boil the LN2 inside causing a considerable explosion. If the dewar engineers aren't recommending it, you should really invest in the sort of dewar meant for this kind of purpose.

comments.text: Over 20 years ago I worked on a contract for Praxair. I worked on a gas cabinet controller. One of the gasses it has to work with was silane. The idea of a welding bottle full of that stuff is terrifying, but not the worst it had to deal with. It also had to work with HFl, the gas form of hydrofluoric acid, carbon monoxide and lots of other nasty stuff. One interesting thing I learned is that one of the ways that silane is used is with carbon monoxide. In semiconductor fabs, when they want a an insulator or a dielectric they can mask off the parts of the chip that they don't want the insulator or dielectric on and then flow carbon monoxide over the exposed silicon. Carbon monoxide will stick in a molecular level onto the silicon. The chamber can then be purged and cleaned and then silane flowed right up against the wafer. It will react with the carbon monoxide and the silicon to form silicon carbide, an excellent insulator and dielectric. It forms one molecule thick so the process is repeated several times until it's thick enough and then the mask is removed which breaks away all the silicon carbide that formed over the mask.

The lack of bounce from that cube is going to be a combination of the shape and the fact that it was still wet. The flat and irregular surfaces cause a lot of waste of momentum - impact vectors don't line up to the center of the object at all. And the composition is too loose and pliable - you can see from the indents that the calipers left in the sides that the material was still too pliant to spring back on a bounce. The liquid coming out of the center also shows that it was still too wet to bounce - the liquid absorbs a lot of the force, and also means the object is more massive than ideal to be able to bounce with that kind of structure.

If it were fully dry both inside and out, it would be lighter, the fibers would be firmer, and they'd be able to spring back from an impact far better. That would make it a lot bouncier. If you could shape it into a sphere, it would probably work quite well.
